title: La Buy v. Howes Leather Co., Inc.
lead: A district judge sent two complex antitrust actions to a master over every party’s objection, and the Supreme Court upheld extraordinary appellate intervention to restore the judge’s responsibility for the basic disputes.

actors.name: Judge La Buy
actors.role: Northern District of Illinois judge whose reference orders were challenged by mandamus

actors.name: Howes Leather and other respondents
actors.role: Parties to the underlying cases seeking to vacate the references

actors.name: Manufacturers, wholesalers, mail-order businesses, and chain operators

proceedings: District judge ordered broad references and refused to vacate them; Seventh Circuit issued mandamus directing vacatur; Supreme Court affirmed 5–4, leaving antitrust merits for district-court adjudication.
limits: The opinion applies the historical Rule 53(b). It neither bars every use of masters nor creates routine interlocutory review. La Buy is named because of the writ proceeding, not as an alleged antitrust participant.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Two antitrust actions occupied the judge for years before trial
sections.cue: Introduce the underlying parties and unfinished merits.
paragraphs: Two federal antitrust actions began in 1950 in the Northern District of Illinois. Independent retail shoe-repair businesses and wholesalers alleged monopolization, price fixing, and discriminatory prices for shoe-repair supplies against manufacturers, wholesalers, mail-order businesses, and chain operators. They sought injunctions, treble damages, and accountings.

The Rohlfing action eventually involved eighty-seven plaintiffs and six remaining defendants; Shaffer involved six plaintiffs and six defendants when mandamus was sought. District Judge La Buy handled years of amended pleadings, party dismissals, discovery disputes, depositions, hearings, and summary-judgment requests. He had substantial familiarity with both cases, but conspiracy, liability, damages, and injunctive relief remained undecided.

sections.title: The judge ordered references without the parties’ consent
sections.cue: Explain the scope that made this more than a discrete accounting.
paragraphs: When the cases came up for trial resetting in February 1955, counsel estimated that one trial would take six weeks. La Buy asked whether the parties would agree to a master. They did not, but the next day he ordered references on his own initiative, directing a master to receive evidence and report findings of fact and conclusions of law on the general issues.

The orders covered conspiracy, liability, damages, and possible injunctive relief, rather than detailed accounting after a judicial liability determination. La Buy cited severe calendar congestion, complexity, and trial length. The parties deposited about $8,000 as security for costs, but all objected and sought vacatur; compliance with the deposit order did not establish consent.

The then-governing Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 53(b) made references exceptional. In nonjury cases other than matters of account, it required an exceptional condition. When La Buy refused to vacate, the parties sought mandamus in the Seventh Circuit under the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1651(a). That court unanimously accepted its authority in an appropriate case, divided over exercise, and issued writs directing vacatur. La Buy sought Supreme Court review of both appellate power and the claimed abuse of discretion.

sections.title: The majority separated the power to issue mandamus from the reason to use it
sections.cue: Connect prospective appellate jurisdiction to the exceptional remedy.
paragraphs: Justice Clark’s opinion held that a court of appeals with eventual appellate jurisdiction could issue mandamus in aid of that jurisdiction in proper exceptional circumstances. The 1948 recodification had not removed that established auxiliary authority. Ordinary review after final judgment did not categorically exclude a writ, but the existence of power did not make every erroneous discretionary order immediately reviewable.

Here, the breadth of delegation was a clear abuse. A master could assist with specified work; the references instead transferred the central adjudication before the judge had decided conspiracy or liability. Clark considered the arrangement nearly an abdication of judicial function, depriving the parties of the trial before the court contemplated by the rule.

La Buy’s years of preparation and antitrust experience strengthened the conclusion. He knew the pleadings, defenses, discovery, and much of the expected proof. Complexity did not establish that a newly appointed substitute would decide the disputes better or faster. Prior decisions restraining improper references and the courts’ responsibility to enforce procedural rules supported intervention beyond an ordinary arguable management choice.

sections.title: Congestion and complexity did not make wholesale referral exceptional
sections.cue: Include the local history and the accounting qualification.
paragraphs: The Seventh Circuit had repeatedly warned that references should be rare and justified by unusual circumstances. La Buy had made eleven references during the preceding six years. The Supreme Court did not find a fully documented circuitwide policy, but considered those admonitions and practice relevant to supervisory intervention. It acknowledged that naming judges in writ proceedings was undesirable and mandamus should remain extreme.

Calendar congestion was common enough that accepting it alone would make referral routine, defeating the rule. Other methods of assignment and pretrial administration might help, adapted to local circumstances. The Court recognized the burden without treating it as permission to replace judges wholesale.

Antitrust complexity and length also did not suffice. Those features favored decision by an experienced regular judge rather than a temporary appointee ordinarily lacking comparable judicial experience. The entitlement to judicial determination of basic issues did not diminish with difficulty.

A limited later accounting was different. After deciding overall liability, the judge might properly assign detailed proof and calculations of individual losses to a master when receiving and tabulating them did not warrant the judge’s time. The ruling therefore allowed specialized assistance while rejecting these transfers of the entire litigation.

sections.title: Brennan would require the parties to wait for final judgment
sections.cue: Explain the dissent’s jurisdictional boundary and practical concern.
paragraphs: Justice Brennan, joined by Justices Frankfurter, Burton, and Harlan, dissented. He distinguished an erroneous exercise of jurisdiction from exceeding or refusing jurisdiction. Rule 53 entrusted La Buy with deciding whether exceptional conditions existed; an incorrect conclusion ordinarily remained error within that authority and could be reviewed after final judgment.

For Brennan, the All Writs Act protected appellate jurisdiction conferred elsewhere rather than independently authorizing review of otherwise unappealable interlocutory orders. The references would not prevent later Seventh Circuit review. Expense and delay were consequences of Congress’s finality policy, not enough to evade it. A transfer outside the circuit could threaten prospective jurisdiction in a way these orders did not.

Brennan distinguished precedents involving the Supreme Court’s historically different mandamus power and wholesale disregard of governing rules. He feared the majority effectively created discretionary interlocutory appeals without Congress and would worsen congestion through petitions and trial delays. He did not regard the reference orders as immune from review, but would reserve correction for ordinary final-judgment appeals.

sections.title: The writs stood while the antitrust merits remained open
sections.cue: State the actual affirmance and its confined reach.
paragraphs: On January 14, 1957, the Supreme Court affirmed the Seventh Circuit 5–4. La Buy had to vacate the broad reference orders, leaving the antitrust actions for proper district-court adjudication. The Court decided neither antitrust liability nor damages and did not bar a properly limited accounting reference.

The majority approved exceptional supervisory intervention on this record. Finding a Rule 53 error did not by itself create a general entitlement to immediate appellate correction of every interlocutory ruling.
